L01:
FlagShip raised a $4.2M seed. Basis Ventures led it.

Eighteen months ago we started building a feature-flag platform, and the pitch hasn't changed since: most teams treat flags as a debugging bolt-on, and that's why their releases are scary.

I'll argue the stronger version of that. Your flag layer sets your release cadence. If turning a change off means a rollback and a hotfix, you batch your work and release when everyone can watch, then call the batching discipline. Teams that can switch a feature off for one customer stop treating release day as an event at all.

Six of us built this. The round pays for more engineers and for the rough edges our early customers keep routing around instead of complaining about.

We're hiring. If you've owned a release process and it annoyed you enough that you wanted to rebuild it, my DMs are open.
L02:
We finished the migration off the monolith this week. Nine months, three teams, p99 latency down 40%.

The 40% is what people quote back at me, and it's the least interesting part. We're a fintech. Our actual problem was that three teams shared one deploy, so the slowest review in the building set everybody's release date.

Writing the services was the easy half. Agreeing on where one service ends and the next begins meant deciding who owns what, and ownership is a political question in an architecture costume. That argument cost more energy than any code we wrote.

Two things I'd tell anyone starting one of these. Draw the boundaries around the domain, not around the technology you happen to like this year. And go incrementally, because big-bang cutovers fail late, which is the expensive kind of failing.

People call microservices overhyped. Usually those people already work somewhere teams ship without waiting on each other. If yours wait, the split buys you something real, and 40% off your tail latency is the smallest part of it.
L03:
We're hiring our first designer. AI startup in Austin, 0.5 to 1% equity, reports to the CEO.

Being the first design hire is a different job from being a designer. No system to work inside. Nobody to review your work, and nobody who can tell you which of your instincts are wrong. Plenty of very good designers would hate that, and if you want a brief handed to you, this role will make you miserable.

What you'd own: what the product looks like, how it behaves, and what we mean when we say something feels finished. That last one isn't a poster on a wall. It's an argument you'll have with engineers most weeks about what actually ships.

The equity range is in the post because I'd rather disagree about the number now than after four calls.

Austin preferred. I'll bend for the right person, and I'd rather not.

If that's the job you want, message me. Send work, not a resume.
L04:
I was laid off in January from a big tech company. Six months later, I'm leading product at a 30-person startup.

In between: 200-plus applications. That number isn't a badge. It's evidence that I spent months doing the thing that scales worst, and I kept doing it because sending an application feels like progress on a day when nothing else does.

The hard part wasn't money. It was that I stopped being sure I was good at my job, which is a strange thing to lose when none of your skills changed on the day you were let go.

I won't tell you rejection is redirection. Most of mine meant someone else fit better. Calling that destiny would have made the next month worse.

A few hiring managers sent real rejections with an actual reason in them. Everyone else sent a form or silence. Those notes took them a couple of minutes to write and I still remember who wrote them.

If you're in the middle of this right now, my DMs are open and I answer them.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same three foundation models. I say that as someone who thinks a few of them will still be worth a lot of money.

A prompt isn't a moat. It's a text file. A competitor can reconstruct it from your product in an afternoon, and if they can't be bothered, one of the model vendors will ship your headline feature at their next launch event.

So what survives that? Two things. How deep you sit in a workflow, meaning how much of a team's week runs through your product and how ugly the week gets when they try to leave. And the data you pile up that nobody else can get, the kind that comes from watching your own users correct your output.

Everything else is a demo, and demos get cheaper every quarter. That's the real shift: the demo can't be the pitch anymore.

The test I'd apply to your own startup is simple. If all three model providers shipped your best feature tomorrow morning, what's still standing on Monday?
L06:
Back from SaaStr Annual. I talked to more than 40 founders, and the useful part wasn't on stage.

Nobody has AI pricing figured out. Not one person I asked. Seats, usage, outcomes, some hybrid invented for one large account that now can't be unwound. The only confident answers came from founders who had shipped their pricing recently enough that no renewal had tested it yet. If your board is asking why you haven't picked a model, this is the year to say you're still measuring.

PLG has gotten boring, in the good way. Product-led growth used to be an argument about whether self-serve works. Now it's an argument about when a rep should appear in the funnel, which is a much better thing to be arguing about.

Community-led growth is back, and this time finance is in the room. Every community program I heard about had a number attached. A few years ago attaching a number would have been treated as missing the point.

Forty-odd conversations, one honest summary: most of us are guessing. The good ones are guessing on purpose.
L07:
Roughly seven in ten enterprise AI pilots never reach production. The models aren't the reason.

The models have been good enough for a while. What they meet on arrival is a company whose data sits in systems that disagree about what a customer is, where the number everyone trusts comes from a spreadsheet one person maintains by hand. No model fixes that, and every pilot finds it out the same way.

Then there's the part nobody budgets for. A pilot that works still asks people to do their job differently, and the process it plugs into was designed around the old constraint. Bolt AI onto that workflow and you get the same output with an extra step and a license fee.

So the pilot demos beautifully and then dies at the point where somebody has to change who approves what.

The companies with AI in production did the boring work first. Fix the data, redesign the process, then buy the model. In that order. It costs you two slow quarters and it's the only order that works.

Technology stopped being the constraint a while ago. We're the constraint, and that's a harder budget line to get approved.
L08:
Clearlens v2 shipped today. Two features: session replay and funnel comparison.

Both came out of more than 300 customer interviews, which is a slow and slightly humbling way to build a roadmap. We walked in with a list of things we were sure people wanted. Most of that list is still on the floor.

Session replay is the feature everyone asks for and plenty of teams use badly. Watching an hour of recordings feels like research and mostly confirms what you already believed. It earns its keep next to the funnel, where you can watch the specific people who dropped at the step you're worried about instead of a random sample of everybody.

That's why the two shipped together rather than one this quarter and one next.

Fourteen beta customers ran it for months and broke it in ways our own tests never did.

The uncomfortable part of building this way: your customers already know what your roadmap should be, and finding out costs you most of your own ideas. Link in the comments if you want to see it.
L09:
Ten years in B2B sales and the skill I'd still rank first is listening.

Here's the call that convinced me. A deal was coming apart. The prospect started listing concerns and every instinct I had said to answer them one by one, fast, because that's what a good rep does.

I said nothing for ninety seconds instead.

Ninety seconds is longer than it sounds, and all of it was excruciating. But the prospect kept talking, worked through the objection out loud, and then named the real blocker, which wasn't on the list and which I'd never have guessed.

We closed two weeks later.

Most people take "ask better discovery questions" from a story like that. I think that's still the wrong instinct, because a question steers. The best information I've gotten in this job showed up when I stopped steering and let someone finish a thought they hadn't finished out loud in front of anyone before.

Reps talk to fill a silence that isn't theirs to fill. Sit in it.
L10:
I'm shutting down Cartful after three years. We raised $1.1M, got to 4,000 users, and never found revenue that repeated.

Three things I'd tell myself at the start.

Users aren't customers. Four thousand signups made every investor update easy to write and covered up the question I didn't want to ask, which was who pays for this and why they'd pay again next month.

One-off deals aren't a sales motion. They feel like traction because they come with all the same paperwork. If you can't say your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one, you have a run of favors.

Runway is for learning, not for staying alive. We stretched ours to survive, and stretching is the most expensive way to spend it, because you buy months instead of answers.

To the people who backed us, worked here, and used the thing: thank you. I'm sorry we didn't get there.

That's the post. There's no line at the end that makes three years and $1.1M come out even.
L11:
We killed the daily standup for a team of 14. Meetings dropped by six hours a week and shipping speed didn't move.

That second number is the one worth arguing about. If you remove a daily meeting from 14 engineers and output stays flat, the standup wasn't doing the thing we all said it was doing.

What replaced it is an async written update. Every morning each person posts what they did, what they're on, and what's blocking them. It's searchable, so I stopped being the routing layer for questions that had already been answered twice, and the people two time zones away stopped learning things a day late.

My honest read on why standups survive. They're a status meeting for the manager, dressed as collaboration. The manager gets a daily feeling of visibility, and 14 people pay for it in broken mornings.

Some teams should keep theirs. Mid-incident, or four people deep in one gnarly problem, talk constantly. Daily, forever, by default, for everyone: no.

Six hours a week is a real line item. Nobody prices it. I have never once watched a team run that number before deciding to keep the ritual for another year.
L12:
Passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional. Eleven weeks of studying, five practice exams, a full-time job the whole way through.

The five practice exams did more for me than any video course. Each one found something I was confident and wrong about, which is the only kind of gap that hurts you on this exam. If you buy one thing, buy the question bank.

Building beat reading, every time. Service docs tell you what a feature does. They don't tell you what it costs you at 3am, and this exam is written by people who know the difference.

An hour a day for eleven weeks beat the eight-hour Saturday. It isn't close. I put the hour on my calendar as a meeting, because the things on my calendar are the things that survive a busy week.

One thing I'd say to anyone deciding whether it's worth it: this exam rewards judgment over recall more than any cert I've taken. That's the part people underestimate, and it's why cramming the service list doesn't get you there.
L13:
A year ago I became an engineering manager. The hardest part wasn't the meetings.

It was losing any way to prove I'd worked. For years my week ended in merged PRs. Now a good week looks like seven people being unblocked and growing, with no artifact anywhere that has my name on it.

That took months to stop feeling like fraud, and I don't think the feeling was irrational. My output really had gone invisible. My mistake was reading invisible as absent.

Three things I got wrong early.

I kept picking up tickets to feel productive. That isn't helping. That's taking the interesting work away from the person who needed it to grow.

I gave people context in the order I thought of it rather than the order they needed it. Most of what I filed as a performance problem that year was a communication problem in disguise, and the missing communication was mine.

And I stayed quiet in the moments where a decision would have cost me something. Ambiguity is comfortable for the manager and expensive for all seven of them.

One year in. Better than I was, worse than I want to be.
L14:
Our nine SREs started writing runbooks. Pages dropped 30% in one quarter.

The systems didn't improve in that quarter. Same code, same infrastructure, same bugs. What changed is that the fix for a recurring alert stopped living in one person's head, so whoever was on call at 2am could close it out instead of waking up the one human who knew.

Four rules made it stick. Every incident ends with a runbook entry or the incident isn't closed. Every repeat page triggers a review of the doc that failed to prevent it. We delete stale docs as hard as we write new ones, because a wrong runbook at 2am is worse than no runbook at all. And runbook quality counts toward our definition of done, which is the only reason any of this survived a busy quarter.

Nobody gets promoted for this. That's a real problem and writing a blog post about it doesn't solve it, so we made it part of the work instead of a virtue.

If your team is drowning in pages, the answer probably isn't another tool.
L15:
We went hybrid after three years fully remote. Two days a week in the office.

Retention improved. Two senior people quit over the policy. Both are true and I've stopped presenting that as a paradox.

The retention number is real, and it's also the least persuasive thing I can tell you, because I can't separate the office days from everything else we changed that year. Anyone who claims they've isolated the effect of a hybrid policy is doing worse math than they think.

The two who left weren't marginal people. They'd built their lives around a remote job, we changed the terms after three years, and they made a rational call. Filing that under culture fit would be a lie I'd have to keep telling.

What I'd tell another leader: pick the model you can defend out loud, then give the actual reason. We told our team it was about onboarding and cross-team work, because it was. The version where you announce it as what your people asked for is the one that costs you trust, and everyone smells it inside a week.

Some days the office is half empty. That's a policy still needing work, not a scandal.
L16:
AI isn't replacing junior developers. It's changing what junior means, which matters more for how you hire.

We hired two juniors this year. Both use AI pair-programming tools all day, and both ship production code faster than a junior would have five years ago. That part isn't close.

What changed is where their hours go. Less on syntax and boilerplate. Much more on reading code they didn't write and deciding whether it's right, which is a reviewing skill we used to say you earned later, after years of writing the code yourself.

So a hiring rubric built on syntax trivia is dead. If your loop still checks whether a candidate can produce boilerplate from memory, you're screening for the first skill that got automated.

Mentorship matters more now, not less. Judgment doesn't autocomplete. A junior who can generate five plausible designs and can't rank them is more dangerous than one who worked slowly and asked.

Companies that stopped hiring juniors because of AI think they cut a cost. They cut their senior pipeline, and that bill arrives later, on somebody else's watch.
L17:
A customer who churned came back last week.

They told us why they left, on the way out, which is rarer than it should be. Our seat-based pricing charged them more every time they hired somebody, and half those seats sat unused. We were billing them for headcount and calling it value.

So we moved to usage-based pricing. It was the most frightening decision we made that year. We modeled the downside a dozen times and some advisors told us plainly not to do it.

Expansion revenue is up 22% since.

The part I'd argue about with other founders: pricing isn't only a revenue lever, it's a statement about whose side you're on. Seat pricing paid us when a customer overbought. Usage pricing pays us when the product gets used. One of those survives a procurement review in a bad quarter.

I don't think it's right for everyone. If your value doesn't scale with usage, you'll add variance to the forecast and irritate your own finance team for nothing.

But if a customer has ever told you they're paying for licenses nobody opens, that isn't a discount conversation.
L18:
Someone I've been mentoring for six months signed an offer this week. Frontend developer at an insurance company.

The work was theirs. What I did was show up weekly, review real code instead of exercises, and run four mock interviews, each one harder than the last.

Two things worth knowing before you agree to mentor somebody.

The value isn't your expertise. It's your consistency. Most weeks there was no visible progress, and the whole job on those weeks was showing up anyway, so that quitting stayed slightly less attractive than continuing.

And review real work. Toy exercises produce toy feedback. The first time we opened their actual project we found problems a course would never surface, because a course doesn't know which shortcuts you personally take.

The industry keeps debating whether bootcamp grads can make it. That debate is mostly about hiring managers, not about grads. This one interviewed well and got hired at an insurance company, which is a harder door to get through than a startup and nobody hands out credit for it.

One hour a week. Go find someone.
L19:
We changed one subject line and opens went up 31% across 18,000 subscribers.

Before: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." After: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking." Same email, same list, same send time. One line names a feature, the other names an outcome the reader already wants.

I've been doing this long enough to be embarrassed by that result. Every marketer knows customers don't care about features. We write feature subject lines anyway, because the feature is what we just shipped and shipping it is what we're proud of. Your subject line is where your internal priorities leak out.

One caveat, because these posts always skip it. A 31% lift on opens is a lift on opens. It is not revenue. Curiosity gets the envelope opened, and if what's inside doesn't pay off the promise, you've taught 18,000 people to distrust your subject lines in exchange for one good week.

We rewrote the rest of the lifecycle emails on the same principle and the gains held. I still care more about the click number.

Go read your last ten subject lines. Count how many are about you.
L20:
Twelve people, no ops function, five tools.

Linear holds anything with a state. If work isn't in Linear it doesn't exist, which sounds harsh until you've spent a Monday reconstructing what everyone agreed to in a thread.

Notion holds anything written down. Docs, onboarding, decisions.

Slack, with aggressive channel hygiene. Slack is the tool most likely to quietly become a second job.

Figma, where an idea has to survive contact with a screen before anyone writes code for it.

Otto is our deploy bot. We built it ourselves and it takes a PR to production with one command. Writing your own deploy tooling is usually a mistake, and this is the exception I'd defend, because deploys are the workflow we touch most and the one we most wanted to shape ourselves.

The rule underneath all of it: every tool charges rent. Licenses are the cheap part. The expensive part is a third place where a decision might be written down.

We add a tool when not having it hurts more than the rent. That's a higher bar than most teams set.
L21:
I took two weeks off. First real break in four years.

The first few days I checked my phone out of habit and felt guilty about it. Nothing broke while I was gone, and I want to be careful about how I say that, because the version of this post where the company hums along beautifully without me is a humblebrag. Things waited. None of them mattered by the second week back.

The useful part came after. With two weeks of distance I looked at my calendar and could finally see how much of it I'd built myself. I killed three recurring meetings in my first week back. Nobody has asked about any of them since.

Which raises a fair question about the four years I spent sitting in them.

I'm not going to claim that rest makes you more productive. That framing is the problem, because it treats rest as an input to output. Take the time because four years without any is too long, and because the calendar you defend when you're exhausted is never the calendar you'd design.
L22:
We hired employee number 50 this week. Three years ago there were four of us in a garage in Denver.

The garage wasn't charming. It was cold, we worked on folding tables next to a space heater, and the whiteboard came off Craigslist.

What I actually think about at 50 people: the thing that got us here doesn't scale, and pretending otherwise is how companies get worse right after they get bigger. At four people everyone hears every customer call. At fifty, most people never hear one, and now that has to be built on purpose or it just stops happening.

The three lines from that Craigslist whiteboard still hold. Customers first. Default to transparency. Hire people better than you are. The last one is free to say at four people and it costs something at fifty, because it means handing work you're good at to somebody who'll do it differently.

To the 46 who joined after us, and to the 900 customers paying for all of it: thank you.
L23:
Networking events are mostly useless, and I went to a lot of them before I decided that.

Conferences, mixers, founder happy hours. Hundreds of business cards. Zero clients.

My last three clients all came from writing online. All three arrived already knowing how I think, which is a different conversation from the one that starts at a badge table.

Writing wins on three counts. It reaches thousands while a conversation reaches one. It selects, so the wrong people filter themselves out before they ever email you. And it compounds: a good post keeps working for months, while a handshake is forgotten by Monday.

I'll grant the obvious objection. Relationships close deals and I'm not claiming otherwise. My point is narrower. Events are a poor way to start relationships and a decent way to maintain the ones you have, and most people attend for the first reason.

Events also feel productive in a way writing doesn't. You come home tired holding a stack of cards. That feeling is the product being sold to you.

Publish the thing instead.
L24:
I was on Supply Chain Weekly, episode 142, talking about AI demand forecasting.

The number we spent the most time on: forecast error down 18% at one of our pilot customers. One customer. I say it that way because this industry turns a single pilot into a category claim, and then everybody wonders why the next deployment disappoints.

What 18% buys isn't a nicer dashboard. It's less overstock and fewer stockouts, and working capital that stops sitting on a shelf.

We also got into the parts that don't demo well. Data quality is still the whole game. If your item master disagrees with your order history, no model saves you, and you'll spend the first quarter of any project finding that out the slow way.

The claim I'll defend: your forecasting team matters more with AI, not less. A model hands you a number. Somebody still has to know the number is wrong because of a promotion that isn't in the system yet. Cut the planners after buying a forecasting tool and you own a very confident number with nobody left who can challenge it.

Link to the episode in the comments.
L25:
ARR went from $1.2M to $3.4M. The team went from 9 to 21. NPS came in at 61.

The mistake I'd take back: we hired sales reps before the founders could close reliably ourselves.

It looked like the responsible move. Demand was there, the founders were the bottleneck, and hiring is what you do about a bottleneck. What we actually did was hand reps a job with no playbook, then review them against targets built on a motion nobody had run twice. They missed. They got frustrated. None of that was their fault.

You can't hand off a sales process you haven't written down. Everyone knows that sentence. I knew it, said it, and it still cost us months.

We rebuilt the process from scratch, wrote down what actually closes, and then it started working.

On the NPS: I like 61 more than I like the ARR line. Growth like ours on unhappy customers is something you can do for exactly one year.

That's the honest version. Most year-in-review posts on your feed today are missing this paragraph.
